items.note: Story 1: Association organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose president 1889-1911, creamery 1891.
Story 1: paid by pounds of butterfat 'ascertained by test'; 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.

Section A says only that the station test was final. It never says that payment by weight would have made the fault cost nothing. The mechanism appears only in B3 and G, which cannot be credited here.
Story 1: Loomis secretary 1901-, Teague bookkeeper 1905-, Sill buttermaker (Larrow Green per Stories 2 and 4).
Story 1: Selby Vose, Gideon's son, manager 1913-1938.
Story 4: yearly station-gain line of 'five and a quarter per cent, as usual'; the 1898 entry is quoted; fat received exceeds fat credited.
Stories 1-2: built winter 1895-96, seven miles up the valley, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed of Larrow Green.
Story 1: weighed, sampled, fixed 17.6 c.c. charge, acid, hand tester, reading; cream to Larrow Green, skim returned. Core process present.
Story 2: Ammon & Sons, Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in use 1 May 1897 (1898 rejected).
Story 2 invoice table: 6 doz pipettes at 17.6 c.c., 12 doz bottles, acid measure, tester, freight, $77.93.
Stories 3 and 6: gap the same 0.19 in July as in February in every year; 'the gap was flat'.
Never says a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, or that there was none in the county. Only mentions that Strawn was issued burettes in 1921.
Story 1: Keddie 1861-1934, twenty-nine seasons 1896-1924, put out 30 April 1925.
Test book, its first leaf and summary leaf are described; kept in his own hand (Story 8).
Story 1 summary leaf: 1896 3.80; 1898 3.61 and within 0.03 every year after.
Story 3: broke 8 May, borrowed measure until 10 July, nine weeks at 3.80, '?' entry.
Story 5: Emmet's sister Orra married Ansel; tester was brother-in-law to the patron who lost most.
Story 8: 1919 circular signed by Vose alone; 17 March 1925 statement that he could not explain the figures and never took cream.
Story 8: died February 1934 with the charge still on him.
Stories 1 and 5: six farms of Hessel Bottom, a wet meadow; Brant's the largest.
Story 5: weigh book from 1 January 1897; the two weights always agreed.
Complaints from 1902 (Story 1). Gaps kept apart: Roy's 0.17 = 3.78-3.61 against the true shortfall of 0.19 (Story 5).
Story 6: committee under Grigg sampled Jan-Mar only; blamed wet hay, reported as its finding and then refuted.
Story 5: 200,000 lb at 3.42. Proportionality stated in Story 2 ('proportionally short reading') and Story 3 (0.19 = 5% of 3.80).
Story 5: Roy took it over in 1929 and lent it to Ivy in 1958; Hazel after his death in 1962.
Story 7: Jerome Cudd, Alder Corners, Vessey County, over Redlow Ridge. The year does not gate this item; 1913 is handled as a deduction.
Story 7: from 1915 four of the six Bottom farms hauled the summer flush over the ridge, and to the Hollow the rest of the year.
Story 7: independent control; different factory, glass and tester; 'never compared figures with anyone'; Vessey County.
Story 7: the same herds tested about 0.19 lower at the station; sixteen seasons 1915-1930 of hauling. It narrows the short-glass overlap to 8 seasons, but that is context and does not gate.
Story 7: same herds in summer on pasture, where Bulletin 214 found no hay effect; watered milk shows at once in cheese. Kills both explanations.
Story 7: Rosalie is Jerome's daughter, not his niece; in 1958 she had the figures copied for Ivy (16-season table).
Story 2: Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector, circuit from 1907, related to nobody. End year 1936 not given; the contested start year is right.
Story 8: lactometer at every visit and never found added water; told the manager so in 1919.
Story 2: 12 June 1923, burette, 'Condemned the lot'.
Never states that Strawn wrote no figure for the deficiency, made no report beyond the condemnation, or drew no inference.
Story 2: order 28 June, Ammon reply 2 July, new glass July 1923, 1924 average 3.80, nobody connected the two.
Story 2: crate to the loft over the intake room. Story 8: notebooks in the college library since 1947.
Story 8: patrons petitioned in January 1925.
Story 8: Frick's board, 17 March-4 May, three sittings, two in the station weigh room.
Story 8: water (Vose), theft (Teague), hay (1908 report); none accepted.
Story 8 lists the four books. Story 4: Strawn's 1923 notebook was before the board and nobody set it beside the receiving book.
Award of $3,800, 'without admission', charged to the station account is given, but the dismissal is not said to be without a finding against him. That is this item's own aspect beside A3.1.
One fifth is stated, but the award is never tied to the very account where the loss had built up as 'station gain'.
Ivy, born 1931, granddaughter, graduate student at Farland, working with Vaught (Bulletin 471 by Vaught and Keddie).
Section A shows her receiving the records piecemeal but never says she assembled records that had never been in the same room. That synthesis is only in G.
Story 2: found February 1958 in the station loft; nine pipettes survived.
Story 2: 9 March, burette, 16.72 vs 17.6, short 0.88, 95% of mark.
Story 8: 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923, one part in twenty low. Story 2: 3.61/0.95 = 3.80. Story 3: 0.19 is 5% of 3.80.
40M lb over 1898-1922 (Story 1); 76,000 lb and $19,000 at 25c (Story 8); gain of 76,000 lb is the shortfall itself (Story 4).
Story 8: Bulletin 471, October 1958.
Granddaughter.
Ansel to Duncan to Ivy; the great-niece claim is rejected by Falke's own correction.
Second cousins, derived through the first-cousin fathers.
Full vs half siblings left open; the diary pages were not preserved; the degree is the same either way.
Gideon Vose, father.
Article VII, his father's rule, turned the short pipette into lost pay.
'No relationship is established' ... 'A negative cannot be strictly proven'. A lean with an explicit decline counts as an abstention at this location.
Vira and Oram assert it from talk; Duncan denies it.
$19,000; one fifth.
76,000 lb; 5.26% of credited and 5.00% of received, both denominators named.
72 pipettes, 0.88 c.c. each.
26 years 42 days vs 25 full years 1898-1922; the part years are explained.
Cannot be determined; both memories cited, no figure given.
Only the pipette changed, 8 May-10 July.
Tester, herds, pasture, scales, acid and more held constant.
3.80 for nine weeks, back to 3.61 when the glass returned.
Locates the cause in the glass, ruling out milk and man. Limits: no size in c.c., not which glass, etc.
Ledger gain (Teague/Sill), 1911 interval (test book/Falke), 1924 recovery (Strawn's note).
Independence argued by record; the ledger gain and 1911 are named as holding without 1958.
A09 abstention item answered 'No.' as a definite verdict.
Yes, he knew the Hollow tested low (1902 complaints, 1919 circular).
Manager from 1913, signed the ledger sheets, wrote the 1919 circular.

No declared inability to settle, only 'Nothing shows he knew' while leaning on Kyle's account. Gives at most one of the required observations: it misses the two office men answering oppositely, that neither cites a document, and that no Vose statement survives.
E.g. 1908 sampling Jan-Mar (Q), weigh book 1 Jan 1897 (M/Q), Orra born 1866 (A), crate in the loft (M), six farms.
Pairs noticed with tie-breakers: 16.27 (NT-1), 12 July (NT-11, 28 June order), $77.39 (NT-14, line sum), among others.
A04 (U, works books burned 1931), A10 (U, undated print, lost minute book), A06 (U with a stated lean).
Self-refutations: r05 'my own device 1905' over an 1898 entry, r15, r18, r20, r11, r03.
Pipettes 16.72 vs 17.6, 95%; 0.19 = 5% of 3.80; onset 1 May 1897 (1896 read 3.80); end 12 June 1923; nothing else changed.
Water (Vose, Sill) defeated by Strawn's lactometer, Alder Corners and the ledger surplus.
Theft (Teague) defeated by the ledger gain (cream arrived heavy), 1911 and 1924.
Hay (Grigg, Kepp) defeated by Bulletin 214's 0.05 in winter and nothing in summer vs a flat 0.19.
A07 answered with the headline 'No.' (four books only, no glassware). A definite assertion.
A05 headline: 'The best evidence is that he suspected the glass'. A verdict sentence; the later 'cannot be fully reconciled' does not undo it.
142 words.
Test book, weigh book, rival factory's tests, inspector's condemnation, ledger: five series.
No decoy adopted, no wrong headline figure.
Five per cent short, 1897, 76,000 lb/$19,000, 1923, 1958, Ansel Keddie named.

deductions.reason: Corruption: Story 8 asserts as fact that 'The patrons had reckoned their loss at 67,000 lb of fat' (planted 67,000 lb, F080).
Corruption: Story 7 asserts that the Alder Corners factory was built in 1913 ('first vat set' when Rosalie was twelve), and E-b lists 1914 as the wrong value (F055, r10).
Gullibility A01: the E-b list resolves 'Vose-Keddie cousins (Vira, Oram)' as a wrong value broken by Duncan's denial. This is a definite assertion elsewhere on the sheet (collision rule).
Gullibility A09: D2 answers 'No.' to whether the bookkeeper questioned the entries.
Gullibility A07: F answers 'No.' to whether the board examined the glassware.
Gullibility A05: F asserts that the tester suspected the glass, as the headline verdict.
